content: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) refers to a range of permanent birth defects caused by maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy. This spectrum includes, but is not limited to, Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS). Over time, research and clinical experience have demonstrated that prenatal alcohol exposure can result in a variety of effects, including physical, behavioral, and cognitive impairments. Consequently, the term FASD was introduced to encompass FAS as well as other conditions resulting from prenatal alcohol exposure. FASD is not a clinical diagnosis in itself but rather a term describing the full range of disabilities that may arise from prenatal alcohol exposure. Currently, FAS is the only condition within the FASD spectrum that is officially recognized and defined by the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-9 and ICD-10). Other FASD conditions, such as Partial Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (PFAS), Alcohol-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (ARND), Alcohol-Related Birth Defects (ARBD), and Fetal Alcohol Effects (FAE), have evolving definitions and nomenclature. A complete evaluation for FASD requires the assessment of four key features: growth deficiency, characteristic facial features, central nervous system (CNS) damage, and prenatal alcohol exposure. A diagnosis of FAS requires positive findings in all four features. However, CNS damage and prenatal alcohol exposure are the critical elements of the FASD spectrum, and a diagnosis of FASD can be made with positive findings in these two features, even if the condition does not meet the full criteria for FAS. Key Features of FASD 1. Growth Deficiency: Growth deficiency is defined as significantly below-average height, weight, or both, due to prenatal alcohol exposure. This can be assessed at any point in the individual’s lifespan, although birth height and weight are preferred measurements. Growth deficiencies are documented when height or weight falls at or below the 10th percentile on standardized growth charts. The 4-Digit Diagnostic Code further categorizes growth deficiency into severe (≤3rd percentile), moderate (≤3rd percentile for either height or weight), mild (3rd–10th percentile), or none (>10th percentile). Growth deficiency contributes to diagnoses of FAS and PFAS but not ARND or static encephalopathy. 2. FAS Facial Features: Three distinct craniofacial abnormalities are diagnostic of FAS: A smooth philtrum (flattening of the groove between the nose and upper lip). A thin vermilion border (thinning of the upper lip). Small palpebral fissures (shortened eye width). These features are measured using standardized tools, such as the Lip-Philtrum Guide and palpebral fissure length (PFL) growth charts. All diagnostic systems agree on these criteria for assessing facial features. 3. Central Nervous System (CNS) Damage: CNS damage is the primary feature of any FASD diagnosis. Prenatal alcohol exposure, a teratogen, can cause brain damage ranging from gross structural abnormalities to subtle functional impairments. CNS damage is assessed in three areas: structural, neurological, and functional impairments. Structural impairments include observable brain abnormalities, such as microcephaly or agenesis of the corpus callosum, often identified through imaging techniques. Neurological impairments include hard signs (e.g., epilepsy) or soft signs (e.g., impaired motor skills, poor coordination). Functional impairments involve deficits in cognitive, behavioral, or adaptive functioning, often assessed through standardized testing. The 4-Digit Diagnostic Code ranks CNS damage as definite, probable, possible, or unlikely, based on the severity and type of impairment. 4. Prenatal Alcohol Exposure: Prenatal alcohol exposure is determined through interviews with the biological mother or family members, review of prenatal health records, or other reliable sources. Exposure levels are categorized as confirmed exposure, unknown exposure, or confirmed absence of exposure. The 4-Digit Diagnostic Code further distinguishes confirmed exposure into high risk (e.g., blood alcohol concentration >100 mg/dL) and some risk. A diagnosis of FAS is possible even with unknown exposure if other key features are present. Other FASD Diagnoses 1. Partial Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (PFAS): Individuals with PFAS have confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure and CNS damage but may lack growth deficiency or the complete set of FAS facial features. They exhibit functional disabilities similar to FAS but may not look like FAS. Diagnostic criteria include: Growth deficiency (normal to deficient). Two or three FAS facial features. Clinically significant CNS damage in three or more brain domains. Confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure. 2. Alcohol-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (ARND): ARND focuses on CNS damage without requiring growth deficiency or FAS facial features. It is characterized by structural, neurological, or functional impairments in three or more brain domains. Confirmed prenatal alcohol exposure is required for diagnosis. ARND is gaining acceptance as a term to describe FASD conditions with CNS abnormalities or behavioral/cognitive deficits. 3. Fetal Alcohol Effects (FAE): FAE was initially used to describe individuals with brain damage due to prenatal alcohol exposure but without obvious physical anomalies. This term has fallen out of favor due to its perceived minimization of the severity of the condition. 4. Alcohol-Related Birth Defects (ARBD): ARBD refers to congenital anomalies linked to maternal alcohol use but without the key features of FASD. This term is no longer widely used, as these anomalies are not specific to alcohol exposure and are not diagnostic criteria for FASD. Diagnosis and Multidisciplinary Evaluation Diagnosing FASD requires a multidisciplinary approach to assess all four key features. Growth deficiency and FAS facial features are typically evaluated by a trained physician. CNS damage is assessed through psychological, speech-language, and occupational therapy evaluations to identify clinically significant impairments in three or more brain domains. Prenatal alcohol exposure risk is assessed by qualified professionals, such as physicians, psychologists, or social workers. These professionals collaborate to produce an integrated report for diagnosis. Challenges in Diagnosis Most individuals with FASD do not exhibit all features of FAS and fall into other FASD conditions. These individuals may be at greater risk for adverse outcomes due to brain damage without the visual cues of poor growth or FAS facial features. Misdiagnosis as primary mental health disorders, such as ADHD or Oppositional Defiance Disorder, is common, leading to inappropriate treatment approaches. While other FASD conditions may not yet be included in official diagnostic systems, they still result in significant functional impairments due to underlying brain damage.
